title: Given an array of numbers, find the maximum sum of any strictly increasing subsequence. Explain how the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program adapts to maximise sum instead of length, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence (Rising Subsequence with the Largest Total)

s1_definition.profdef: The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence adapts the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program to optimise total value rather than count. We define, for each index, the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends at that index, seeded with the element's own value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. This runs in quadratic time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks at a customer's series of deposit amounts and finds the rising subsequence of deposits, not necessarily consecutive, whose amounts add up to the most money, because the bank rewards growing deposit discipline. The goal is the largest total among strictly rising deposit picks.
s1_definition.oneliner: The best sum ending at an index is its own value plus the best sum ending at any earlier smaller value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence adapts the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program to optimise total value rather than count. We define, for each index, the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends at that index, seeded with the element's own value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. This runs in quadratic time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India looks at a customer's series of deposit amounts and finds the rising subsequence of deposits, not necessarily consecutive, whose amounts add up to the most money, because the bank rewards growing deposit discipline. The goal is the largest total among strictly rising deposit picks.

**One line to remember:** The best sum ending at an index is its own value plus the best sum ending at any earlier smaller value.

sections.s2_technical:
We define a sum array where the entry at index i is the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends with the element at i. We seed each entry with the element's own value, because the element by itself is a valid rising subsequence. For each i we look back at every earlier index j with a strictly smaller value, because such a subsequence can be extended by the element at i, and we take the best extension, which is the element at i plus the best sum ending at j. The answer is the maximum entry overall, since the best rising subsequence may end anywhere.

Bottom-up: `int[] sum = a.clone(); int best = a.length == 0 ? 0 : a[0]; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j] < a[i]) sum[i] = Math.max(sum[i], sum[j] + a[i]); best = Math.max(best, sum[i]); }`. A concrete check: for deposits four, one, three, seven the best sum is four plus seven equals eleven or three plus seven equals ten, so eleven wins. Senior nuance: this mirrors the longest increasing subsequence structure but swaps count for value, so it maximises sum not length, and it stays quadratic because the value objective breaks the tails-array trick that speeds up the length version.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India examines a customer's series of deposit amounts and wants the strictly rising subsequence of deposits, not necessarily consecutive, whose amounts add up to the largest total, because the bank rewards customers whose deposits show growing discipline. Enumerating subsequences is exponential. This is exactly how the Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence works: it finds the largest rising total with the best-earlier-smaller sum recurrence.

The code defines a `DepositRewardService` exposing `maxRisingDepositSum(deposits)` returning the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence. A `Demo` runs it over a sample deposit array and logs the total.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the deposit array four, one, three, seven. We want the largest sum of a strictly rising subsequence.

Step 1 — Each deposit seeds its best sum with its own value: four, one, three, seven respectively.

Step 2 — At three the only earlier smaller value is one, so three can extend it to one plus three equals four, which beats three alone, so the best sum ending at three is four.

Step 3 — At seven several earlier values are smaller: four, one, and three. Extending the sum ending at four gives four plus seven equals eleven. Extending the sum ending at three, which is four, gives four plus seven equals eleven as well. Extending the sum ending at one gives one plus seven equals eight.

Step 4 — The best sum ending at seven is therefore eleven, from the rising subsequence four then seven.

Step 5 — The maximum best sum across all indices is eleven. The answer is eleven. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:30:44 PM com.bank.depreward.service.DepositRewardService maxRisingDepositSum
INFO: Max rising deposit sum = 11
Oct 27, 2026 9:30:44 PM com.bank.depreward.DepositRewardApplication main
INFO: Maximum rising deposit sum is 11
```

```

    │
    ▼
  sum[i] = a[i] + max(sum[j]) over j<i with a[j]<a[i]
    │ 4→4  1→1  3→max(3, 1+3)=4
    │ 7→max(7, 4+7, 4+7, 1+7)=11   (4 then 7)
    ▼
  best = max(sum) = 11
    ▼
  Output: max rising deposit sum = 11
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence is the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program with the objective swapped from counting elements to summing values. For each index I compute the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends at that element, and I seed each index with the element's own value because the single element is a valid rising subsequence on its own.

To extend, I look back at every earlier index holding a strictly smaller value, since the rising subsequence ending there can be continued by the current element, and I take the best extension, which is the current value added to the best sum ending at that earlier index. The answer is the maximum sum over all indices, because the winning subsequence can end anywhere. This stays quadratic in time, and I note that the value objective prevents the tails-array speedup that works for the length version.

At the National Bank of India I used this to examine a customer's series of deposit amounts and find the strictly rising subsequence whose amounts summed to the most, because the bank rewarded customers whose deposits showed growing discipline. I computed the best rising sum ending at each deposit and took the maximum. Explaining that I seed with the element value, extend from the best earlier smaller sum, and take the overall maximum is what shows an interviewer that I understand how to adapt the increasing subsequence pattern to a value objective.
